overview: Databricks Workflows (branded as Lakeflow Jobs in the modern platform) is the native orchestration service that runs multi-task jobs, coordinating notebooks, Python wheels, JARs, DLT/Lakeflow pipelines, SQL, dbt, and nested jobs as a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

It removes the need for an external scheduler for Databricks-centric pipelines by providing task dependencies, retries, conditional branching, loops, triggers, notifications, and repair runs, all managed by the Databricks control plane.

Understanding multi-task orchestration is essential for building reliable, cost-efficient, observable production data and ML pipelines on the lakehouse, and it is a very common senior data engineering interview topic.
learningObjectives: Model a production pipeline as a multi-task Databricks Job using task dependencies (depends_on) to form a DAG.

Choose the correct task type (notebook, python_wheel, spark_jar, dlt/pipeline, sql, dbt, run_job, condition, for_each) and the correct compute model (job cluster vs shared job cluster vs all-purpose vs serverless).
Pass state between tasks with job/task parameters and task values (dbutils.jobs.taskValues), and configure triggers, retries, timeouts, notifications, concurrency, run-as identity, and repair runs.
Define jobs declaratively as code via the Jobs REST API 2.1 and Databricks Asset Bundles YAML for reproducible CI/CD.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: A Databricks Job is a control-plane-managed unit of orchestration composed of one or more tasks arranged in a DAG via explicit dependencies. Each task has a task type, a compute target, parameters, and a retry/timeout policy; the job as a whole has triggers (schedule, file arrival, table update, continuous, or manual/API), concurrency limits, a run-as identity, and notification rules. The Databricks scheduler evaluates dependencies, launches compute, executes tasks in topological order, records run history and lineage, and supports repairing (rerunning) only the failed subset of tasks.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of a Workflow as a recipe with numbered steps where some steps can only start after others finish. Databricks is the head chef: it reads the recipe, spins up the kitchen equipment (clusters) when needed, runs each step in the right order, retries a step that fails, passes small notes between steps (task values), and tells you by email or Slack whether dinner succeeded or burned. If one dish fails, you can redo just that dish instead of cooking the whole meal again (repair run).
coreConcept.historicalContext: Early Databricks jobs supported only a single task per job, so teams chained multiple single-task jobs or relied on external orchestrators like Airflow to build DAGs. In 2021 Databricks introduced multi-task Jobs (Workflows), letting a single job contain a DAG of tasks with shared clusters and dependencies. Since then Databricks added task values, conditional (if/else) tasks, for-each loop tasks, run_job tasks for modular composition, file arrival and table update triggers, serverless compute for jobs, and repair runs. In 2024 Databricks unified its orchestration and ingestion story under the Lakeflow brand, where Workflows became Lakeflow Jobs, while the Jobs REST API and Asset Bundles remain the code-first interfaces.

whyItMatters.business: Reliable, automated pipelines mean fresh, trustworthy data for analytics, BI, and ML products; failures are caught and alerted, reducing SLA breaches and manual firefighting that cost analyst and engineering time.
whyItMatters.engineering: A single native DAG engine eliminates a separate orchestrator to operate, gives first-class lineage and run history, and lets engineers express dependencies, retries, branching, and loops declaratively rather than in glue code.
whyItMatters.scalability: Jobs can fan out with for-each tasks, run many tasks concurrently on ephemeral job clusters, and scale across thousands of scheduled runs orchestrated centrally by the control plane while compute scales elastically in the data plane.
whyItMatters.cost: Ephemeral job clusters (and serverless jobs) spin up only for the run and terminate after, shared job clusters amortize a cluster across sibling tasks, and repair runs re-execute only failed tasks, all of which cut wasted compute (DBUs and cloud VMs).
whyItMatters.reliability: Built-in retries with backoff, task and job timeouts, dependency-aware execution, run_if rules for partial failures, and repair runs make pipelines self-healing and resilient to transient issues without duplicating data when tasks are idempotent.

coreComponents.name: Job and Tasks (the DAG)
coreComponents.definition: A job is the top-level orchestration object; tasks are the individual units of work within it, each declaring dependencies on other tasks via depends_on to form a directed acyclic graph.
coreComponents.purpose: To express a complete pipeline as an ordered graph so the scheduler knows what runs, in what order, and what can run in parallel.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Holds the task list, dependency edges, run_if conditions, per-task and job-level settings; the scheduler executes tasks in topological order and parallelizes independent branches.
coreComponents.examples: A job with tasks ingest -> transform -> {gold_sales, gold_inventory} -> publish, where the two gold tasks run in parallel after transform.

coreComponents.name: Task Types
coreComponents.definition: The kind of work a task performs: notebook_task, python_wheel_task, spark_jar_task, pipeline_task (DLT/Lakeflow), sql_task (query/dashboard/alert/file), dbt_task, run_job_task, condition_task (if/else), and for_each_task.
coreComponents.purpose: To orchestrate heterogeneous workloads (Spark, SQL, dbt, ML wheels, nested jobs) and control flow (branching and looping) inside one job.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Each task type binds to a specific execution engine or control-flow behavior and defines its own required fields (e.g., notebook_path, entry_point, warehouse_id, pipeline_id).
coreComponents.examples: A pipeline_task triggering a DLT pipeline, a for_each_task iterating over regions running a nested notebook, a condition_task branching on a task value.

coreComponents.name: Compute Targets (Job Clusters, Shared Job Clusters, All-Purpose, Serverless)
coreComponents.definition: The cluster or serverless compute on which a task runs; a job cluster is ephemeral and created per task, a shared job cluster is reused across tasks in the same run, an all-purpose cluster is long-lived, and serverless jobs compute is Databricks-managed and instant-on.
coreComponents.purpose: To provide the right cost/latency/isolation trade-off for each task, from cheap ephemeral compute to fast serverless startup.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Defines runtime version, instance types, autoscaling, and lifecycle; job clusters terminate after the run, shared job clusters are declared in job_clusters and referenced by job_cluster_key.
coreComponents.examples: spark_version 15.4.x-scala2.12 with autoscale 2-8 workers as an ephemeral job cluster; a shared job cluster reused by three sibling notebook tasks; serverless compute for a lightweight SQL transform.

coreComponents.name: Triggers and Scheduling
coreComponents.definition: The mechanism that starts a job run: a Quartz cron schedule, a file arrival trigger, a table update trigger, continuous execution, or manual/API/run_job invocation.
coreComponents.purpose: To start pipelines at the right time or in response to the right event without manual intervention.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Evaluates the trigger condition (time window, new files at a path, updated Delta tables, or continuous), respects pause status and max_concurrent_runs, and launches a run.
coreComponents.examples: quartz_cron_expression '0 0 2 * * ?' at 02:00 UTC; a file_arrival trigger polling a Unity Catalog external location; a table_update trigger on a source Delta table.

coreComponents.name: Parameters and Task Values
coreComponents.definition: Job-level parameters and per-task parameters supply configuration at runtime; task values (dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set/get) let one task publish small key/value results that downstream tasks read.
coreComponents.purpose: To parameterize runs (e.g., date, environment) and pass small pieces of state between tasks without external storage.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Job parameters are resolved with defaults and overrides at trigger time; task values are stored by the control plane per run and fetched by downstream tasks or referenced in condition tasks.
coreComponents.examples: Passing {{job.parameters.run_date}} into a notebook; setting dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set('rows', 1200) and reading it with taskValues.get in a later task or a condition_task.

coreComponents.name: Reliability Controls (Retries, Timeouts, Notifications, Concurrency, Repair)
coreComponents.definition: Per-task retry policies with min_retry_interval, task and job timeout_seconds, on_start/on_success/on_failure/on_duration_warning notifications, max_concurrent_runs, run_as identity, and repair runs that rerun only failed tasks.
coreComponents.purpose: To make pipelines resilient, observable, and operable in production.
coreComponents.responsibilities: The scheduler applies retries with backoff, enforces timeouts, sends notifications to email/webhook/Slack/PagerDuty, limits overlapping runs, executes under a chosen identity (user or service principal), and supports repairing a run from the point of failure.
coreComponents.examples: max_retries 3 with a 2-minute interval, a 3600-second task timeout, a Slack webhook on failure, max_concurrent_runs 1 to prevent overlap, run_as a service principal, and repairing only the failed gold task.

internalWorking: When a job is triggered (by schedule, event, API, or manual run), the control-plane scheduler creates a run, resolves job parameters and defaults, and validates the DAG for cycles and referenced compute/pipelines.

The scheduler computes the topological order of tasks; tasks with no unmet dependencies become eligible and are dispatched, launching ephemeral job clusters (or attaching to shared job clusters / serverless) as required.

As each task completes, the scheduler records its state and any published task values, then re-evaluates downstream tasks: a task starts only when its dependencies satisfy its run_if condition (e.g., ALL_SUCCESS, AT_LEAST_ONE_SUCCESS, NONE_FAILED, ALL_DONE).

condition_task nodes evaluate a boolean expression (often over a task value or job parameter) and route execution down the true or false branch; for_each_task expands its inputs into N iterations of a nested task, optionally with bounded concurrency.

On task failure the scheduler applies the retry policy (retries with min_retry_interval and optional retry_on_timeout); if retries are exhausted the task is marked failed, dependent tasks are skipped per run_if, notifications fire, and the run ends in a failed/terminal state that can later be repaired to rerun only failed and downstream tasks.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Trigger (schedule / file arrival / table update / continuous / API) -> Control-Plane Scheduler (resolve params, validate DAG, topological order) -> Launch Compute (job cluster / shared job cluster / serverless) -> Execute Tasks in dependency order (notebook / wheel / jar / pipeline / sql / dbt / run_job / condition / for_each) -> Task Values + State recorded -> Downstream tasks via run_if -> Notifications + Run History/Lineage -> (on failure) Repair Run of failed subset
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A schedule (Quartz cron) fires at 02:00 UTC or a file arrival trigger detects new files; the control-plane scheduler creates a new job run and resolves job parameters such as run_date.
2. The scheduler launches the required compute: an ephemeral job cluster for the ingest task (and a shared job cluster referenced by later sibling tasks), then dispatches the entry (root) task.
3. The ingest notebook reads raw files from cloud storage, writes a Bronze Delta table, and publishes a task value dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set('ingested_rows', count).
4. A condition_task reads the ingested_rows task value; if it is greater than zero it routes to the transform branch, otherwise it routes to a no-op / alert branch.

5. The transform and gold tasks execute (some in parallel), a for_each_task fans out per-region aggregations, notifications fire on success, and the full run history, task durations, and lineage are recorded; if any task failed, an engineer repairs the run to rerun only that task and its descendants.

keyTerminology.meaning: A single unit of work identified by a unique task_key; depends_on lists the upstream task_keys that must complete before it runs, forming the DAG.
keyTerminology.importance: Dependencies define execution order and parallelism; correct task_key wiring is the core of building a correct pipeline graph.

keyTerminology.meaning: A key/value store scoped to a job run that lets a task set small values and downstream tasks (or condition tasks) get them.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables passing state (counts, flags, dynamic paths) between tasks without a database or file, and drives conditional branching.

keyTerminology.meaning: A per-task rule determining when it runs based on upstream results: ALL_SUCCESS (default), AT_LEAST_ONE_SUCCESS, NONE_FAILED, ALL_DONE, AT_LEAST_ONE_FAILED, ALL_FAILED.
keyTerminology.importance: Controls behavior on partial failure, enabling cleanup tasks, fan-in aggregation, and always-run finalizers.

keyTerminology.meaning: Re-executing a failed job run so that only the failed tasks (and their downstream dependents) rerun, reusing prior successful results.
keyTerminology.importance: Saves time and compute by avoiding a full rerun and is a defining operational feature of Databricks Workflows.

keyTerminology.meaning: The identity (a user or, in production, a service principal) under which a job executes and accesses data and resources.
keyTerminology.importance: Decouples pipeline execution from an individual's credentials, essential for production security, governance, and least-privilege access.

importantConcepts.concept: Job Cluster vs Shared Job Cluster vs All-Purpose vs Serverless
importantConcepts.explanation: A job cluster is created for a single task and terminated after, giving isolation and clean cost attribution. A shared job cluster is declared once and reused by multiple tasks in the same run, amortizing startup time and cost across sibling tasks. An all-purpose cluster is long-lived and interactive, generally an anti-pattern for scheduled jobs due to cost and contention. Serverless jobs compute is Databricks-managed, starts in seconds, requires no cluster config, and is ideal for lightweight or bursty tasks; the choice trades startup latency, isolation, and cost.

A run_job_task lets one job invoke another job as a task, enabling reusable sub-pipelines, team ownership boundaries, and DAGs that compose smaller jobs. This keeps individual jobs focused, allows independent scheduling and permissions per sub-job, and supports passing parameters into the child job, at the cost of extra indirection in run history.

variationsAndTypes: **Scheduled batch jobs:** Triggered by a Quartz cron expression on a fixed cadence (hourly, daily) with a timezone.
**Event-driven jobs:** Triggered by file arrival at an external location or by table updates to source Delta tables, running only when new data appears.
**Continuous jobs:** A single always-on run that immediately restarts, used for near-real-time processing (often around Structured Streaming).
**Modular/composed jobs:** Jobs that call other jobs via run_job tasks to reuse sub-pipelines across teams.
**Control-flow jobs:** Jobs using condition (if/else) and for_each loop tasks to branch and fan out dynamically.
advantages: **Native and integrated:** No separate orchestrator to operate; deep integration with clusters, DLT/Lakeflow pipelines, Unity Catalog lineage, and notebooks.
**Rich control flow:** Dependencies, conditional branching, for-each loops, run_if conditions, and modular run_job composition in one DAG.
**Operational resilience:** Retries with backoff, timeouts, notifications, and repair runs that rerun only failed tasks.
**Cost-efficient compute:** Ephemeral job clusters, shared job clusters, and serverless jobs minimize idle spend.
**Code-first and reproducible:** Full definition via Jobs REST API 2.1 and Databricks Asset Bundles YAML for CI/CD and version control.
disadvantages: **Databricks-centric:** Best suited to Databricks-native workloads; orchestrating heavy non-Databricks systems still favors a general-purpose orchestrator like Airflow.
**Limited cross-job global scheduling:** Complex cross-team, cross-platform DAGs may need an external control layer above Workflows.
**Cluster startup latency:** Ephemeral job clusters add cold-start time (mitigated by serverless or pools).
**Task value size limits:** Task values are for small state, not for passing large datasets between tasks.
**Learning curve for control flow:** condition/for_each semantics and run_if rules require care to avoid subtle DAG bugs.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use Databricks Workflows when your pipeline is primarily Databricks-native (notebooks, DLT/Lakeflow pipelines, SQL, dbt, Spark), when you want built-in retries, lineage, cost-efficient ephemeral/serverless compute, repair runs, and code-first definitions via Asset Bundles.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid making it your sole orchestrator when you must coordinate many non-Databricks systems (external APIs, on-prem jobs, complex cross-platform DAGs) where a dedicated orchestrator like Airflow provides richer operators and a single pane of glass; there, trigger Databricks jobs from that orchestrator instead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: A Databricks Workflow is like a factory assembly line with a smart floor manager. Each station (task) does one job and can only start when the parts from earlier stations arrive (dependencies). The manager turns machines on only when a station needs them and off afterward (ephemeral clusters), passes small work orders between stations (task values), sends a page when a station jams (notifications), and, if one station fails, restarts only that station and everything after it rather than the whole line (repair run).

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need Airflow or an external scheduler to build DAGs on Databricks.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Databricks Workflows natively supports multi-task DAGs with dependencies, branching, loops, retries, and triggers. External orchestrators are only needed when coordinating significant non-Databricks systems.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Every task in a job should run on its own new cluster.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Sibling tasks can share a shared job cluster to amortize startup cost, and lightweight tasks can use serverless compute. Always creating a fresh cluster per task wastes time and money.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Scale within a job using for_each tasks with bounded concurrency and parallel branches; scale across jobs by composing with run_job tasks. The control plane orchestrates thousands of runs while ephemeral/serverless compute scales elastically in the data plane. Use max_concurrent_runs to control overlap.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Configure per-task retries with min_retry_interval_millis, retry_on_timeout, task and job timeout_seconds, and run_if conditions so partial failures are handled gracefully. Make tasks idempotent (e.g., Delta MERGE, overwrite by partition) so retries and repairs never duplicate data.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Use repair runs to rerun only the failed subset, always-run finalizer tasks (run_if ALL_DONE) for cleanup/alerts, and continuous jobs with automatic restart for streaming. Persist checkpoints for streaming so restarts resume exactly-once.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track run status, task durations, and lineage in the Jobs UI and via system tables (system.lakeflow / system.billing / system.access). Set on_duration_warning thresholds to catch slow runs before they breach SLAs and alert on repeated retries.
productionConsiderations.security: Set run_as to a dedicated service principal (not a person) so pipelines survive employee changes and follow least privilege. Scope Unity Catalog grants to that principal, restrict job edit/manage permissions via job ACLs, and store secrets in Databricks secret scopes referenced at runtime.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Prefer ephemeral job clusters or serverless over all-purpose clusters, use shared job clusters for sibling tasks, size autoscaling tightly, use spot/preemptible instances where safe, and rely on repair runs to avoid re-executing successful tasks. Tag jobs and clusters for cost attribution.
productionConsiderations.performance: Reduce cold starts with serverless or instance pools, parallelize independent branches, right-size clusters per task, avoid oversized shared clusters, keep task values small, and offload heavy transformation to DLT/Lakeflow pipelines or optimized Spark rather than serial notebook cells.

codeExamples.title: Multi-Task Job Definition via Jobs REST API 2.1 (DAG with dependencies, retries, triggers, notifications)
codeExamples.overview: This creates a production multi-task job through the control-plane Jobs API 2.1. It defines an ingest -> transform -> {gold_sales, gold_inventory} DAG using a shared job cluster, per-task retries, a Quartz cron schedule, a service principal run_as, concurrency limit, and Slack/email notifications.
codeExamples.breakdown: The job declares one shared job cluster (shared_etl) referenced by all four tasks via job_cluster_key, so a single autoscaling Photon cluster serves the whole run. depends_on wires ingest -> transform -> {gold_sales, gold_inventory}; the two gold tasks run in parallel after transform. Per-task max_retries with min_retry_interval_millis add resilience, timeout_seconds caps runaway tasks, run_as ties execution to service principal sp-etl-prod, max_concurrent_runs 1 prevents overlapping runs, and the Quartz cron fires nightly at 02:00 UTC. Notifications go to email on failure and to a preconfigured Slack webhook destination.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A JSON response containing a job_id (e.g., {"job_id": 872455109345}). The job appears in the Workflows/Jobs UI as a four-node DAG, runs nightly at 02:00 UTC, and sends failure alerts to email and Slack.
codeExamples.commonIssues: 401 from an expired token; 400 if a depends_on references a nonexistent task_key or introduces a cycle; run_as failing if the caller lacks permission to run as the service principal; node type unavailable in region; webhook destination id not created in advance under notification destinations.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use a shared job cluster for sibling tasks to amortize startup; enable Photon for CPU-bound SQL/ETL; consider serverless jobs compute to remove cold starts; pin the runtime version for reproducibility; scope the service principal to least-privilege Unity Catalog grants.

codeExamples.title: Databricks Asset Bundle: jobs resource YAML with pipeline, dbt, condition, and for_each tasks
codeExamples.overview: This databricks.yml bundle defines a job declaratively for CI/CD. It shows heterogeneous task types (DLT/Lakeflow pipeline, dbt, notebook), a condition (if/else) task branching on a task value, a for_each loop task fanning out over regions, file arrival trigger, and notifications, all deployable with 'databricks bundle deploy'.
codeExamples.code:
bundle:
  name: sales_platform

resources:
  jobs:
    sales_lakehouse:
      name: sales_lakehouse_${bundle.target}
      max_concurrent_runs: 1
      run_as:
        service_principal_name: sp-etl-prod
      job_clusters:
        - job_cluster_key: shared_etl
          new_cluster:
            spark_version: 15.4.x-scala2.12
            node_type_id: i3.xlarge
            autoscale: { min_workers: 2, max_workers: 6 }
            runtime_engine: PHOTON
      parameters:
        - name: run_date
          default: "{{job.trigger.time.iso_date}}"
      tasks:
        - task_key: ingest
          job_cluster_key: shared_etl
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/bronze_ingest.py
            base_parameters: { run_date: "{{job.parameters.run_date}}" }
          max_retries: 3
          min_retry_interval_millis: 120000

        - task_key: bronze_check
          depends_on: [ { task_key: ingest } ]
          condition_task:
            op: GREATER_THAN
            left: "{{tasks.ingest.values.ingested_rows}}"
            right: "0"

        - task_key: dlt_silver
          depends_on: [ { task_key: bronze_check, outcome: "true" } ]
          pipeline_task:
            pipeline_id: ${resources.pipelines.silver_pipeline.id}

        - task_key: dbt_gold
          depends_on: [ { task_key: dlt_silver } ]
          dbt_task:
            project_directory: ../dbt
            commands: ["dbt deps", "dbt run --select gold"]
            warehouse_id: ${var.sql_warehouse_id}

        - task_key: per_region_reports
          depends_on: [ { task_key: dbt_gold } ]
          for_each_task:
            inputs: "[\"us\", \"eu\", \"apac\"]"
            concurrency: 3
            task:
              task_key: region_report
              job_cluster_key: shared_etl
              notebook_task:
                notebook_path: ../src/region_report.py
                base_parameters: { region: "{{input}}" }

        - task_key: finalize
          depends_on: [ { task_key: per_region_reports } ]
          run_if: ALL_DONE
          notebook_task:
            notebook_path: ../src/finalize.py
            job_cluster_key: shared_etl
      trigger:
        file_arrival:
          url: s3://acme-landing/sales/
      email_notifications:
        on_failure: [ data-oncall@acme.com ]
        on_duration_warning_threshold_exceeded: [ data-oncall@acme.com ]
      health:
        rules:
          - metric: RUN_DURATION_SECONDS
            op: GREATER_THAN
            value: 5400

variables:
  sql_warehouse_id:
    description: SQL warehouse for dbt
    default: 0abcd1234efgh567
codeExamples.breakdown: The bundle deploys a job whose graph is: ingest -> bronze_check (condition on the ingested_rows task value) -> dlt_silver (only on the 'true' outcome) -> dbt_gold (dbt run on a SQL warehouse) -> per_region_reports (a for_each loop over us/eu/apac with concurrency 3) -> finalize (run_if ALL_DONE so it always runs for cleanup/alerting). It mixes pipeline_task, dbt_task, notebook_task, condition_task, and for_each_task. A file_arrival trigger starts the job when new files land in the S3 landing path, and a health rule plus on_duration_warning notification catch slow runs. ${bundle.target} makes names environment-specific for dev/stage/prod.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Running 'databricks bundle validate' passes, and 'databricks bundle deploy -t prod' creates/updates the job. The Jobs UI shows the branching DAG; the job runs whenever files arrive in s3://acme-landing/sales/ and skips the DLT branch when ingested_rows is 0.
codeExamples.commonIssues: for_each inputs must be a JSON string; referencing a task value that the upstream task never set; condition_task outcome edges must use outcome: 'true'/'false'; dbt task needs a valid warehouse_id and project_directory; pipeline_id must resolve (define the pipeline resource or hardcode an existing id); file arrival triggers require the URL to be a Unity Catalog external location the run_as principal can read.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep bundle targets (dev/stage/prod) to promote the same code with different variables; use ${resources...} references so pipeline/job ids are wired automatically; bound for_each concurrency to protect downstream systems; commit the bundle to Git and deploy via CI so job definitions are versioned and reviewable.

codeExamples.title: Passing state between tasks with dbutils.jobs.taskValues (set/get) and job parameters
codeExamples.overview: This Python notebook code shows the producer task publishing task values and reading job parameters, and the consumer task reading those values. Task values drive the condition_task branching used in the previous examples and let tasks hand small state to each other without external storage.
codeExamples.code:
# ---------- Task: ingest (producer) ----------
# Read the job parameter passed at runtime (with a safe default)
dbutils.widgets.text("run_date", "")
run_date = dbutils.widgets.get("run_date")

bronze_df = (
    spark.read.format("json")
    .load(f"s3://acme-landing/sales/{run_date}/")
)
count = bronze_df.count()

(
    bronze_df.write.format("delta")
    .mode("overwrite")
    .option("replaceWhere", f"event_date = '{run_date}'")  # idempotent partition overwrite
    .saveAsTable("main.bronze.sales")
)

# Publish small task values for downstream tasks / condition tasks
dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="ingested_rows", value=count)
dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key="bronze_path", value="main.bronze.sales")
print(f"Ingested {count} rows for {run_date}")

# ---------- Task: transform (consumer) ----------
# Read a value published by the upstream 'ingest' task; debugValue is used
# when running the notebook interactively outside a job context.
ingested_rows = dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(
    taskKey="ingest", key="ingested_rows", default=0, debugValue=0
)
bronze_path = dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(
    taskKey="ingest", key="bronze_path", default="main.bronze.sales", debugValue="main.bronze.sales"
)

if ingested_rows == 0:
    dbutils.notebook.exit("No rows ingested; skipping transform")

silver_df = (
    spark.table(bronze_path)
    .dropDuplicates(["order_id"])
    .filter("amount > 0")
)
silver_df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("main.silver.sales")
print(f"Transformed {silver_df.count()} rows from {bronze_path}")
codeExamples.breakdown: The ingest task reads the run_date job parameter via a widget, writes Bronze using replaceWhere for an idempotent partition overwrite (so retries/repairs never duplicate data), then publishes ingested_rows and bronze_path as task values. The transform task calls dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get with taskKey pointing at 'ingest'; default handles a missing value in a job and debugValue lets the notebook run interactively without a job context. The ingested_rows value is exactly what the condition_task in the bundle example compares against 0 to decide whether to run the silver branch.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: In a job run, transform reads ingested_rows (e.g., 12034) and bronze_path from the ingest task and processes Silver; when run interactively, it uses debugValue (0), exits early, and prints the skip message. Task values are visible in the run's task details in the Jobs UI.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting debugValue causes errors when running the notebook outside a job; task values must be small JSON-serializable values, not DataFrames; getting a value from a task that did not set it returns the default; widgets not declared before get raise errors; using taskValues in non-notebook tasks requires the appropriate SDK approach.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep task values tiny (counts, flags, table names, paths), not data; always provide default and debugValue for portability; use idempotent writes (replaceWhere/MERGE) so retries and repair runs are safe; reference task values in condition tasks to branch cheaply rather than launching heavy compute to decide.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An e-commerce company must refresh its sales lakehouse every morning so BI dashboards and an ML demand-forecasting model have fresh, validated data by 6 AM. The pipeline spans ingestion, transformation, gold aggregation, per-region reporting, and a downstream ML job, and it must be reliable, cost-efficient, alert on failure, and rerun only what failed after an incident.
endToEndExample.inputData: Nightly JSON order files landing in s3://acme-landing/sales/<date>/ (partitioned by event_date), a Unity Catalog external location over the landing bucket, and existing Bronze/Silver/Gold Delta tables in the 'main' catalog.
endToEndExample.architecture: A single multi-task Databricks Job (Lakeflow Job) orchestrates the DAG: ingest (notebook) -> bronze_check (condition on ingested_rows task value) -> dlt_silver (DLT/Lakeflow pipeline) -> dbt_gold (dbt on a SQL warehouse) -> per_region_reports (for_each over us/eu/apac) -> train_forecast (run_job task invoking the ML training job) -> finalize (run_if ALL_DONE). Sibling notebook tasks use a shared Photon job cluster; dbt uses a SQL warehouse; the job is deployed via a Databricks Asset Bundle, runs as service principal sp-etl-prod, is triggered by file arrival, and caps max_concurrent_runs at 1.
processingSteps: 1. New files land in s3://acme-landing/sales/<date>/; the file arrival trigger starts a run and resolves run_date from the trigger time.
2. The ingest notebook writes Bronze with an idempotent replaceWhere partition overwrite and publishes the ingested_rows task value.
3. The bronze_check condition_task compares ingested_rows > 0; if false it skips downstream and routes to finalize (alerting an empty load), if true it proceeds.
4. dlt_silver runs the DLT/Lakeflow pipeline applying expectations to build validated Silver; dbt_gold then builds Gold marts on a SQL warehouse.

5. per_region_reports fans out with a for_each task (concurrency 3) generating regional reports, train_forecast invokes the ML job via a run_job task, and finalize runs with run_if ALL_DONE to send a completion summary; on any failure, engineers use a repair run to rerun only the failed task and its descendants.
endToEndExample.output: Validated Bronze, Silver, and Gold Delta tables in the 'main' catalog; three regional report tables; a refreshed forecasting model; and a completion summary. Full run history, per-task durations, task values, and Unity Catalog lineage are recorded.
endToEndExample.monitoring: The Jobs UI shows the DAG, per-task status, and durations; system.lakeflow and system.billing tables track run metadata and cost; an on_duration_warning threshold and a health rule (RUN_DURATION_SECONDS > 5400) flag slow runs; repeated retries surface as warnings to on-call.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Each task has retries with min_retry_interval and a timeout; idempotent writes (replaceWhere / DLT / MERGE) make retries safe. run_if ALL_DONE ensures finalize always runs to alert on partial failure. If dbt_gold fails after retries, the run ends failed, on-call is alerted via email and Slack webhook, and a repair run reruns only dbt_gold, per_region_reports, train_forecast, and finalize, reusing the successful ingest and dlt_silver results.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Dashboards and the forecasting model are refreshed and validated before 6 AM every day. Compute cost is minimized via a shared Photon job cluster and a SQL warehouse used only during the run, failures alert on-call immediately, and post-incident recovery is fast because repair runs re-execute only the failed subset rather than the entire pipeline.

industryUseCases.problem: Hundreds of nightly ETL and reporting pipelines across regions must run in dependency order, retry on transient failures, and refresh dashboards before business hours without an army of on-call engineers.
industryUseCases.solution: Model each domain as a multi-task Databricks Job with shared job clusters, for_each fan-out over regions, retries/timeouts, file arrival triggers, and Slack alerts; deploy all jobs as Asset Bundles through CI/CD with a service principal run_as.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reliable dependency-aware execution, parallel regional processing, fast repair runs after incidents, and lower compute cost from ephemeral/shared clusters, with all definitions version-controlled.

industryUseCases.problem: Near-real-time viewing events must be processed continuously and then feed hourly aggregation and recommendation-refresh jobs, coordinating streaming and batch in one pipeline.
industryUseCases.solution: A continuous job runs the Structured Streaming ingestion with checkpointing, while a scheduled multi-task job uses run_job tasks to compose aggregation, feature engineering, and model-refresh sub-jobs with table update triggers.
industryUseCases.benefits: Low-latency ingestion with automatic restart, modular reusable sub-jobs per team, and event-driven downstream runs that only execute when source tables actually change.

industryUseCases.problem: Regulated end-of-day pipelines must run under a controlled non-human identity, enforce timeouts and audit trails, branch based on data validation outcomes, and recover quickly after failures without reprocessing everything.
industryUseCases.solution: Multi-task jobs run as a dedicated service principal with Unity Catalog least-privilege grants, use condition tasks to branch on validation task values, enforce task/job timeouts and health rules, and rely on repair runs and always-run finalizers for controlled recovery and alerting.
industryUseCases.benefits: Strong governance and auditability, deterministic branching on data quality, bounded run durations for SLA compliance, and rapid, minimal-scope recovery via repair runs.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Scale within a job with for_each loop tasks (bounded by a concurrency setting) and parallel independent branches; scale across jobs by composing sub-jobs with run_job tasks so teams own and scale their pieces independently. The control-plane scheduler orchestrates large numbers of concurrent runs while job clusters and serverless compute scale elastically in the data plane; max_concurrent_runs governs how many runs of the same job overlap.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Per-task retries (max_retries, min_retry_interval_millis, retry_on_timeout) recover from transient errors; run_if conditions (ALL_DONE, NONE_FAILED, AT_LEAST_ONE_SUCCESS) control downstream behavior on partial failure; repair runs rerun only failed and downstream tasks. Idempotent writes (Delta MERGE, replaceWhere, streaming checkpoints) guarantee retries and repairs never corrupt or duplicate data.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Databricks operates the control-plane scheduler with regional redundancy and an SLA. Deploy data-plane clusters across multiple availability zones so autoscaling and recovery survive AZ failures; use continuous jobs with automatic restart for always-on streaming workloads, and serverless compute to remove single-cluster dependencies.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Define all jobs as code via Asset Bundles / Jobs API and store them in Git so a workspace's orchestration can be redeployed in another region. Replicate Delta data (deep clone or cloud replication) and version notebooks via Repos; keep secret scopes and service principals reproducible via Terraform so a job can be reconstructed and repointed after a regional outage.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Use shared job clusters for sibling tasks to avoid repeated cold starts, serverless or instance pools to cut startup latency, and Photon for CPU-bound SQL/ETL. Parallelize independent branches, keep task values tiny, right-size autoscaling, and push heavy transformation into DLT/Lakeflow pipelines or optimized Spark rather than long serial notebooks.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Prefer ephemeral job clusters, shared job clusters, or serverless over long-running all-purpose clusters; use spot/preemptible workers where interruption-tolerant; enable aggressive auto-termination; leverage repair runs so re-execution touches only failed tasks; and tag jobs/clusters for cost attribution. Remember the bill splits into Databricks DBUs plus underlying cloud VM/storage cost.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Run production jobs as a dedicated service principal (run_as) with least-privilege Unity Catalog grants, not a personal account. Control who can view/manage/run each job via job ACLs, store credentials in secret scopes referenced at runtime, restrict file arrival triggers to authorized external locations, and keep run-as identity separate from job-authoring identity for separation of duties.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use the Jobs UI DAG view, run history, and per-task metrics; query system tables (system.lakeflow.jobs / job_run_timeline / task_run_timeline, system.billing.usage, system.access.audit) for programmatic monitoring and cost analysis; wire notifications (on_start/on_success/on_failure/on_duration_warning) to email, Slack, PagerDuty, or generic webhooks; and set health rules on run duration to catch regressions.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Enforce quality inside tasks: DLT/Lakeflow pipeline expectations, Delta constraints, and explicit checks in notebooks that publish a pass/fail task value. Use a condition_task to branch on that value so bad data halts or quarantines the pipeline rather than propagating, and record validation metrics for auditing.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Configure notifications on failure and duration-warning to on-call channels; centralize run logs and audit events to a SIEM via system tables or log delivery; alert on repeated retries, unexpected long durations, and jobs that skip branches due to failed data validation; keep a runbook mapping each alert to a repair-run recovery procedure.

recommendedPractices: **Define jobs as code** with Databricks Asset Bundles (or the Jobs API) and store them in Git so orchestration is versioned, reviewed, and promoted through dev/stage/prod targets.
**Run production jobs as a service principal** (run_as) with least-privilege Unity Catalog grants rather than a personal account.
**Make every task idempotent** (Delta MERGE, replaceWhere, streaming checkpoints) so retries and repair runs never duplicate or corrupt data.
**Use ephemeral or shared job clusters (or serverless)** instead of all-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs to control cost and contention.
**Configure retries, timeouts, notifications, and run_if conditions** on every production task so failures are handled and surfaced, not silent.
engineeringStandards: All production jobs must set explicit max_retries, timeout_seconds, max_concurrent_runs, and on_failure notifications.
Every job must run as an approved service principal and be deployed via CI, never edited ad hoc in the UI for production.
Sibling tasks that can share compute must use a shared job cluster; lightweight tasks should prefer serverless.
Data-quality-gating condition tasks must exist before any task that publishes data to consumers.
designRecommendations: Keep individual tasks small and single-purpose; compose larger pipelines with run_job tasks for modularity and ownership.
Use condition tasks to branch on validation results and for_each tasks to fan out over partitions/regions with bounded concurrency.
Add an always-run finalizer task (run_if ALL_DONE) for cleanup, summary, and alerting on partial failure.
Parameterize runs (dates, environments) via job parameters and pass small state via task values, never large data.
namingConventions: Name jobs by domain, cadence, and environment (e.g., sales_lakehouse_daily_prod).
Use descriptive task_keys that read as a pipeline (ingest, bronze_check, dlt_silver, dbt_gold, finalize).
Name shared job clusters by role (shared_etl, shared_ml) and reference via job_cluster_key.
Tag jobs and clusters with team, cost-center, and pipeline tags for billing attribution.
documentationStandards: Document each job's DAG, trigger, run-as identity, and SLA in a README next to its bundle.
Document task values produced/consumed and condition-task branch logic so behavior on partial data is clear.
Maintain a runbook mapping each alert to a repair-run recovery procedure.
Record required Unity Catalog grants and secret scopes for the service principal.
testingStrategies: Validate bundles in CI with 'databricks bundle validate' and deploy to a dev target before prod.
Test task values and condition branching by injecting zero-row and normal inputs.
Test retry and notification behavior by deliberately failing a task in a dev job.
Verify idempotency by rerunning/repairing a task and asserting no duplicate rows are produced.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running scheduled jobs on long-lived all-purpose clusters instead of job/serverless compute.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It is convenient to reuse an interactive cluster that is already running, and teams avoid cold-start latency.
commonMistakes.impact: Idle all-purpose clusters run up cost, cause resource contention between interactive users and jobs, and lose per-run isolation and clean cost attribution.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use ephemeral job clusters, shared job clusters for sibling tasks, or serverless jobs compute; reserve all-purpose clusters for interactive development only.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming tasks are idempotent, so retries and repair runs duplicate or corrupt data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Tasks use plain append writes or non-deterministic logic without considering that the scheduler may run a task more than once.
commonMistakes.impact: Retries and repair runs create duplicate rows or inconsistent state, silently poisoning downstream analytics and models.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Write idempotently with Delta MERGE, replaceWhere partition overwrite, or streaming checkpoints so any rerun converges to the same correct result.

commonMistakes.mistake: Passing large data between tasks via task values or notebook exit strings.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Task values are a convenient way to hand information downstream, so teams overload them.
commonMistakes.impact: Hitting size limits, serialization errors, and brittle pipelines; task values are meant for small state, not datasets.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Persist data to Delta tables and pass only small references (table names, paths, counts, flags) via task values; use tables/volumes for actual data handoff.

commonMistakes.mistake: No retries, timeouts, or failure notifications on production tasks.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Jobs are prototyped without operational hardening and shipped to production as-is.
commonMistakes.impact: Transient failures cause full-pipeline failures, runaway tasks hang indefinitely, and no one is alerted until dashboards go stale.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Set max_retries with min_retry_interval, task/job timeout_seconds, and on_failure/on_duration_warning notifications on every production task.

comparisonSection.explanation: Job clusters are created for the run and terminated after, giving isolation and clean cost attribution; a shared job cluster is reused by sibling tasks to amortize startup. All-purpose clusters are long-lived and interactive, generally an anti-pattern for jobs due to idle cost and contention. Serverless jobs compute is a third option with near-instant startup and no cluster management.

A repair run re-executes only the failed tasks and their downstream dependents, reusing prior successful results to save time and compute. A full rerun re-executes everything from the start, wasting resources and delaying recovery; repair runs are the preferred recovery mechanism when tasks are idempotent.

Databricks Workflows is native, integrated with clusters, DLT/Lakeflow, Unity Catalog lineage, and repair runs, with no separate system to operate, ideal for Databricks-centric pipelines. Airflow offers richer operators and a single pane of glass across many non-Databricks systems; it is preferred when orchestrating heavy cross-platform DAGs, often triggering Databricks jobs from within it.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is a multi-task job in Databricks Workflows?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It is a single job containing multiple tasks arranged as a DAG via dependencies (depends_on). The scheduler runs tasks in dependency order, parallelizing independent ones, and each task can be a notebook, Python wheel, JAR, DLT pipeline, SQL, dbt, nested job, condition, or for-each task.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that one job can express a whole pipeline as a graph, replacing chains of single-task jobs and, for Databricks-native work, an external orchestrator.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you define the order in which tasks run?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Each task declares depends_on listing the upstream task_keys it waits for; this forms the DAG. A task becomes eligible when its dependencies satisfy its run_if condition (default ALL_SUCCESS). Tasks with no unmet dependencies run in parallel.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Shows understanding of depends_on and run_if as the mechanisms defining execution order and parallelism.

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you pass information between tasks, and what are the limits?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Use task values: a task calls dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key, value) and a downstream task calls dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey, key, default, debugValue). Values must be small, JSON-serializable state (counts, flags, table names, paths). For actual datasets, write to Delta tables and pass only references.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Highlights task values for small state, the debugValue for interactive runs, and the anti-pattern of passing large data through them.

intermediateQuestions.question: Compare job clusters, shared job clusters, all-purpose clusters, and serverless for jobs.
intermediateQuestions.answer: A job cluster is ephemeral per task with isolation and clean cost attribution. A shared job cluster is declared once and reused by multiple tasks in a run to amortize startup. All-purpose clusters are long-lived/interactive and an anti-pattern for scheduled jobs. Serverless jobs compute is Databricks-managed with near-instant startup and no config. The trade-off is startup latency vs isolation vs cost vs management.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A strong answer maps each option to a cost/latency/isolation trade-off and recommends ephemeral/shared/serverless for production jobs.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain repair runs and why idempotency matters for them.
advancedQuestions.answer: A repair run re-executes only the failed tasks of a run and their downstream dependents, reusing prior successful results rather than restarting the whole job, which saves time and compute. Because a task may be retried or repaired, each task must be idempotent (Delta MERGE, replaceWhere overwrite, streaming checkpoints) so reruns converge to the same correct state without duplicating data. run_if ALL_DONE finalizers still run to alert/clean up on partial failure.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Ties together repair runs, retries, run_if, and idempotent writes as the reliability story of Workflows.

advancedQuestions.question: How do condition tasks and for_each tasks change the DAG, and how are they typically used?
advancedQuestions.answer: A condition_task evaluates a boolean (often over a task value or job parameter) and routes execution down a 'true' or 'false' outcome edge, enabling if/else branching such as skipping downstream work when zero rows were ingested. A for_each_task takes a JSON array of inputs and runs a nested task once per input, with a concurrency bound, enabling fan-out over regions/partitions. Both add control flow beyond simple linear dependencies while keeping the graph acyclic.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Demonstrates knowledge of modern control-flow tasks and realistic use cases (data-quality gating and fan-out).

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your nightly pipeline of 8 tasks fails at task 5 due to a transient warehouse error. Dashboards must be ready by 6 AM and you cannot afford to rerun the first 4 heavy tasks. How do you recover, and how do you prevent this in future?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Recovery should avoid re-executing successful heavy tasks, so use a repair run of the failed subset. Prevention needs retries with backoff on transient errors, timeouts, idempotency to make reruns safe, and alerting so on-call reacts fast. Consider serverless/shared clusters to reduce cold-start delays that eat into the SLA.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Trigger a repair run so only task 5 and its downstream tasks (6-8) rerun, reusing tasks 1-4's results, meeting the 6 AM SLA. To prevent recurrence, add max_retries with min_retry_interval and retry_on_timeout on the warehouse-dependent task, set sensible timeout_seconds, ensure each task is idempotent (MERGE/replaceWhere) so repairs are safe, configure on_failure and on_duration_warning notifications to on-call, and consider serverless or a shared job cluster to cut cold-start latency.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a production-grade, code-managed orchestration for a multi-team lakehouse where teams own domain pipelines that must run in dependency order, handle data-quality gating, fan out per region, run under governed identities, and recover quickly from failures.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Each domain team defines its pipeline as a multi-task Databricks Job in a Databricks Asset Bundle stored in Git, deployed via CI to dev/stage/prod targets. A top-level orchestrator job composes domain jobs with run_job tasks to express cross-domain dependencies. Within each job, use notebook/DLT/dbt tasks, condition tasks for data-quality gating on task values, for_each tasks for per-region fan-out, shared job clusters or serverless for compute, and run_if ALL_DONE finalizers. All jobs run_as domain service principals with least-privilege Unity Catalog grants; triggers use file arrival or table update; notifications go to Slack/email; system tables feed a monitoring dashboard.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Composing with run_job tasks improves modularity and ownership but adds indirection in run history. Shared job clusters cut cost but reduce isolation between tasks; serverless removes cold starts but changes cost characteristics. Native Workflows avoids operating Airflow but is less suited to heavy non-Databricks systems, where an external orchestrator triggering Databricks jobs may be layered on top.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Scale within jobs via for_each concurrency and parallel branches; scale across teams via independently deployed run_job-composed sub-jobs; let the control-plane scheduler handle many concurrent runs while ephemeral/serverless compute scales in the data plane. Use max_concurrent_runs to bound overlap and spread clusters across AZs for resilience.

followUpQuestions: How do file arrival and table update triggers differ from a cron schedule, and when would you use each?
What run_if conditions exist and how do they change behavior on partial failure?
How would you monitor job cost and duration programmatically using system tables?
When would you choose an external orchestrator like Airflow over native Workflows?
How do continuous jobs support near-real-time streaming and how do they recover after a restart?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Databricks Workflows (Lakeflow Jobs) is the native multi-task orchestration service that runs heterogeneous tasks as a DAG with dependencies, triggers, retries, control flow, notifications, and repair runs, managed by the control plane.
keyConcepts: Job = DAG of tasks wired by depends_on; run_if controls when a task runs (ALL_SUCCESS default).
Task types: notebook, python_wheel, spark_jar, pipeline (DLT), sql, dbt, run_job, condition (if/else), for_each.
Compute: ephemeral job cluster, shared job cluster (job_cluster_key), all-purpose (anti-pattern), serverless.
Task values (dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set/get) pass small state; job parameters parameterize runs.
Triggers: Quartz cron schedule, file arrival, table update, continuous, manual/API/run_job.
Reliability: retries + timeouts + notifications + max_concurrent_runs + run_as + repair runs.
formulas: Quartz cron format: seconds minutes hours day-of-month month day-of-week [year] (e.g., '0 0 2 * * ?' = 02:00 daily).
for_each concurrency: number of iterations run in parallel out of the total input array length.
commands: POST /api/2.1/jobs/run-now  # trigger a run with optional parameters
POST /api/2.1/jobs/runs/repair  # repair (rerun) only failed tasks of a run
databricks bundle validate | deploy -t prod | run <job>  # Asset Bundles CLI
dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set(key='k', value=v)  # publish a task value
dbutils.jobs.taskValues.get(taskKey='t', key='k', default=d, debugValue=d)  # read a task value
interviewPoints: depends_on forms the DAG; run_if governs partial-failure behavior.
Repair runs rerun only failed tasks and require idempotent writes.
Prefer job/shared/serverless clusters over all-purpose for scheduled jobs.
Task values carry small state only; datasets go through Delta tables.
Define jobs as code via Jobs API 2.1 or Asset Bundles; run_as a service principal.
quickNotes: condition_task branches on true/false outcome edges; for_each_task fans out over a JSON array.
Always provide default and debugValue in taskValues.get for portability.
Use run_if ALL_DONE for always-run finalizer/cleanup/alert tasks.
Set on_failure and on_duration_warning notifications to email/Slack/webhook.
File arrival and table update triggers run jobs only when new data appears; continuous jobs auto-restart.

keyTakeaways: Databricks Workflows (Lakeflow Jobs) is the native orchestrator that runs multi-task jobs as a DAG, wiring heterogeneous task types (notebook, wheel, JAR, DLT pipeline, SQL, dbt, run_job, condition, for_each) with depends_on and run_if.

Choose compute deliberately: ephemeral job clusters and shared job clusters (via job_cluster_key) or serverless for scheduled jobs, avoiding long-lived all-purpose clusters that waste cost and cause contention.
Pass small state between tasks with task values (dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set/get) and parameterize runs with job parameters; persist actual data to Delta tables and pass only references.

Harden production jobs with retries, timeouts, notifications, max_concurrent_runs, a service-principal run_as, idempotent writes, and repair runs that rerun only the failed subset for fast, low-cost recovery.

Define jobs as code via the Jobs REST API 2.1 or Databricks Asset Bundles YAML, deploy through CI/CD across dev/stage/prod, and use triggers (cron, file arrival, table update, continuous) to run pipelines exactly when needed.
